record.tranche_reason: The study uses probes, layer-execution interventions, and a residual-state transfer—not a difference-in-means refusal direction—to examine whether harmful-intent recognition and refusal behavior can dissociate.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the original refusal-direction study but does not extract, ablate, add, or weight-edit that direction. SafeDepth’s benchmark gains come from a safety-trained routing method and are not evidence that the claimed direction caused those gains. Rows below capture the paper’s explicit layer-routing safety interventions and its harmfulness/readout and refusal-control analysis; unrelated capability and SafeDepth benchmark comparisons are omitted.
record.test_reason: Appendix A.4 tests whether harmful intent and refusal dissociate. It uses per-layer linear harmfulness probes, counts harmful outcomes despite a positive danger margin, and flips single later-layer execute/skip decisions while harm stays readable. This is a different method aimed at V5's question. No difference-in-means refusal direction is extracted, ablated, added or weight-edited, so V1–V4 and V6–V8 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with one omission: the Q4 analyses are run on an adaptive layer-skipping checkpoint (FlexiDepth on Llama-3-8B-Instruct), not on plain Llama. The authors conclude harmful intent is readable in intermediate states while later execution decisions still decide refusal. Their main contribution is SafeDepth, a safety-aware router that cuts unsafe responses and false refusals relative to FlexiDepth.
record.recipe_differences: No difference-in-means direction is extracted or edited. The study probes harmfulness, changes execute/skip decisions at selected layers, and transfers a residual state; its main method is safety-aware token-level routing.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effects vary with inference phase (prefill versus decoding), restored layer, and evaluation benchmark. At layer 18, the reported outcome also differs between decode-only restoration and restoration in both phases.

fits_no_version.finding: Adaptive layer-skipping raises harmful-response rates over the backbone. Restoring skipped layers changes safety in ways that depend on phase (prefill vs decoding), layer and benchmark.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which layers execute, and in which inference phase, changes refusal and safety behavior beyond the amount of computation, separately from any single refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing the layer-16 final-token residual with a harmful donor's adds a refusal-like preface while the benign task is kept. A self-transfer control reproduces the native answer and a same-norm random replacement does not add the preface.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A harmful-request residual state can induce refusal framing without changing the task being answered.

record.problems: The paper does not test the claimed refusal direction. The reported probe AUROC and route-intervention counts have no uncertainty estimates stated in the text. The cross-prompt transfer is a single illustrative case; the paper also reports illustrative paired intervention examples and a strict evaluator-agreement subset.
record.rows_left_out: SafeDepth and baseline benchmark tables, task-capability results, and component ablations were not extracted because they evaluate the paper’s safety-aware routing method or general capability rather than the refusal-direction mechanism. The paper gives qualitative XSTest comparisons for some adaptive models in Appendix A.1 without values in the prose; no separate rows were made for those statements.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction is extracted, ablated or added; capability under ablation is not tested.
No test that jailbreaks suppress a refusal direction, and no adversarial training against ablation.
No comparison of single-direction, affine, cone or multi-direction accounts.

No harmfulness direction is compared with a refusal direction. There is no steering along a harm direction and only one (adaptive) model is tested. Evidence comes from linear probe readout plus layer-skip interventions, not from representations in an unmodified full-depth model.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.
No manipulation of how or when refusal training is done.

record.verdict_notes: The study's subject in Q2–Q4 is an adaptive model whose skipped layers are replaced or removed, so the refusal changes reflect damaged computation rather than the normal model's mechanism. V5 support is suggestive: probe readout, two examples and small paired counts, with no uncertainty reported. The paper cites Arditi et al. only in related work. SafeDepth benchmark results are method performance and do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction is found, ablated, or added; capability preservation under that ablation is not tested.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The paper does not test whether attacks suppress a refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
It does not compare single-direction, affine, cone, or multiple-direction descriptions of refusal.
The study examines harmfulness readout, later routing decisions, and one residual transfer in Llama-3-8B-Instruct; it does not identify a harmfulness direction or test the claim across models.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer of a refusal direction is tested.
The paper trains a safety-aware router, but does not test how refusal-alignment training timing or method determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.
No reasoning-model test of the refusal-direction claim is reported.

relation.reason: Appendix A.4 reports the study's own results on whether harm readout and refusal dissociate.

tranche.reason: Q4 tests a V5 question: does recognising harmful intent determine refusal? It uses per-layer linear harm probes plus single-layer execute/skip interventions and a residual transfer. This is a different method from difference-in-means, aimed at the same question.

source_check.notes: The layer-16 probe sits upstream of FlexiDepth's routed layers (17-32), so 'harm stays readable' under later-layer flips holds by construction. A harm probe may also read the refusal direction itself. The counts are tiny with no uncertainty. The Table 8 cross-prompt residual transfer (layer 16, with self-transfer and same-norm random controls) bears on V5; check that a row records it.

statements.correction: arXiv:2610.00815: FlexiDepth layer-skipping checkpoint of Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Skipping one later prefill layer (routed layers 17-32) flips 6 prompt-layer pairs from refusal to harmful compliance; 170 refusal pairs unchanged; executing one skipped layer flips 1 pair back (strict two-evaluator agreement). Harm readout is a layer-16 linear probe (AUROC 0.946), upstream of all routed layers. No harm-side removal.
statements.problem: The visible text gives no numbers for this study (the statement is cut off). The conditions list residual carriers, heads, weights and SAE features, not this study's layer skipping. The study removes only the refusal side (skipping one later layer); it never removes a harm side. r1 is a probe, not a removal.

statements.correction: arXiv:2610.00815: FlexiDepth adaptive checkpoint of Llama-3-8B-Instruct; of 200 harmful prompts (set not named), 62 have a positive layer-20 probe danger margin yet end in a harmful answer; no comparison count or uncertainty.
statements.problem: r2 does show harm readable while refusal fails. But the shift here is architectural (adaptive layer skipping in a FlexiDepth checkpoint), not language, syntax, tool or jailbreak. The study is not in the conditions, the prompt set is unnamed, and the visible text gives no numbers for this study.
